the metal pen
•
the east new york yard is home to the J, L, M and Z trains. pretty much everything here is all new technology trains (ntt), with the L primarily using R143 cars (J/Z sometimes also), all lines using R160 cars and the J/Z using R179 cars. it’s a pretty busy yard on a daily basis, with trains shuffling in and out of service. 
•
among the R160s, R143s and R179s we see in revenue service today, sitting amongst them all is the R211T, the newest order of subway cars for the mta, being really close to revenue service as we speak. the R211 sets at this time were still doing testing around the east new york curve, performing clearance testing to see if it works (it does work). right now at this time it’s signed up to jamaica center, being either a J or a Z. but soon enough, we’ll see them among the masses of trains in service today. just give it some more weeks. don’t quote me on that.
•

posts.caption_text: A famous little boomer locomotive of the northwest is Lorane Valley Lumber number 1. The tiny wood-burning 0-4-0T saddle-tank was built as a 2-4-2T by H. K. Porter Co., construction number 1236, in January of 1891 for the Rogue River Valley Railway of Medford, Oregon. In 1905 she was sold to the Skelly Lumber Co. of Yoncalla, Oregon, where she likely lost her pilot and trailing truck to improve her traction. In 1912 she was sold to the J. H. Chambers Lumber Co. of Cottage Grove, Oregon. This line became the Lorane Valley Lumber in 1946, and number 1 continued in yard service until being sold to Mrs. Chadwell O'Connor of Alta Loma, California as a birthday gift for her husband in 1952. Acquiring the name "Sespe" but retaining the number 1, this locomotive was in limited tourist service for many years, and is now on display where her career began in Jacksonville, Oregon. #porterlocomotive #loggingrailroad #railyard #oregonhistory #lumbercompany #steam #train #trains #locomotive #railroad

[LINK IN BIO] Bill Daniel, Phoenix, AZ 2014. Bozo Texino tattoo by Dan Higgs! Bill answered a few questions about buZ blurr for Fluke 11 back in 2013. This new issue has a full interview with Bill, a personal hero of mine since 1992, when I read his article “Who is Bozo Texino?” in Cometbus issue 27. So yes, it’s truly an honor to have him in issue 18. We talked about zines, Aaron Cometbus, buZ blurr and monikers, among other things. Susan A. Phillips—also interviewed in Fluke 18—had this (and more) to say about him: “Bill is genius-level smart. His work has been central to the formation of this entire freight train moniker world, fandom and all. He’s basically a cult figure in the world of moniker writing. He carries a lot of respect in the art world in general. His Bozo Texino film really put him on the map. When you pay attention to small things, like Bill does, you learn a great deal about the world and its workings.”
